summary: Both round-4 majors are genuinely fixed, and I measured the fix rather than reading it. In a copy of the staged tree, deleting each `< 0` half individually turns :format:test red for all four fields (streamCount, podCount, podLen, partitionId), and probing shows each is an accept-flip, not a reworded refusal: the negStreamCount object decodes to a checkpoint with no streams, negPodCount to one with no pods, negPodLen to pods={p=7}, and the partitionId splice to a fully valid checkpoint at partition 1. The two false equivalence arguments are gone from baselines/mutants.txt. The five remaining arguments all hold: I ran each mutation (divisor removed, divisor /9, podCount doubled, podLen widened to Integer.MAX_VALUE, each requireNonNull deleted) and all six survive as claimed, and I probed the gap inputs each argument depends on -- streamCount=3 with 40 bytes remaining, podCount=5 with 4, podLen=5 with 2, podLen=0x7ffffff0 with 2 -- and every one is still refused with an IOException, only the message changing. The 19-byte minimum stream entry and 2-byte minimum pod entry make that exhaustive rather than sampled, and Cursor.bytes bounds before allocating so the widened podLen bound cannot reach the OutOfMemoryError the guard exists for. Nothing here touches an object-store request. Four minors, none blocking; three of them are false sentences about the tree rather than defects in it, which is what this file's own contract is about.

findings.summary: The header's account of the remedy is wrong for one of the four fields it claims. It says all four `< 0` halves are 'now KILLED by objects crafted to end exactly after the field under test', and CheckpointDecodeRefusalTest.java:287-292 still kills the partitionId half with `spliceAt(single, FIRST_STREAM + 16, WIDE_NEGATIVE)` -- a wide varint spliced into the middle of a complete valid checkpoint, which is exactly the technique the same paragraph names three sentences earlier as the thing that produced the false podCount claim. The kill itself is real and I measured it: with `partitionId < 0 ||` deleted those bytes are ACCEPTED as Checkpoint[sequence=1, streams={RunKey[11112222-3333-4444-0000-000000000001, partitionId=1]=StreamOffsets[90, 10]}, pods={poda=1}], and the `hasMessageContaining("partitionId")` assertion is what catches it -- the splice happens to be safe here because replacing one byte with ten leaves the object still ending exactly at its last field. So the substance holds and only the stated mechanism does not. CheckpointDecodeRefusalTest.java:249 carries the same overreach ('EACH OBJECT ENDS EXACTLY AFTER THE FIELD UNDER TEST') in a method whose fourth object is a splice, then silently narrows to 'ALL THREE' seven lines later.
findings.failure_scenario: A fifth narrowing field is added to decodeBody. Its author reads baselines/mutants.txt for how the four existing ones are pinned, is told the splice technique was eliminated in favour of hand-built objects, and follows the partitionId assertion instead -- which is the technique the file says was removed. If the new field's splice does not happen to preserve the object's end, the trailing-bytes check fires either way and the guard is unconstrained again, which is precisely finding M4.8a-r4-2 reintroduced by the prose written to close it.

findings.summary: The requireNonNull entry is right that both mutants survive and right that neither flips refuse into accept -- I confirmed both by running them -- but its stated reason, 'new LinkedHashMap<>(null) raises NullPointerException either way', does not hold for every input, and it is the only entry in the file whose argument is not 'the same objects are refused, only the message differs'. Measured in a copy of the staged tree with `Objects.requireNonNull(pods, "pods")` deleted: `new Checkpoint(-1, Map.of(), null)` throws IllegalArgumentException: sequence is never negative: -1, where the staged code throws NullPointerException: pods. The deleted check runs BEFORE the `sequence < 0` check at Checkpoint.java:71, so for a caller that gets two arguments wrong the exception CLASS changes, not just its message. Both still refuse and nothing is accepted, which is why this is minor rather than the blocking category the file reserves for a wrong equivalence claim -- but the entry as written is stronger than what I could measure.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.8b writes a checkpoint and its caller catches NullPointerException to distinguish 'a map was not populated' from 'the sequence counter went wrong'. Someone deletes the parameter check on this entry's licence, and the null-map case now surfaces as IllegalArgumentException about the sequence whenever the sequence is also invalid -- an operator chasing a counter bug that does not exist.

findings.summary: 'One entry per mutant' is still contradicted by the file's own entries, which is the half of finding M4.8a-r4-5 that was reworded rather than fixed: the first entry covers two mutants ('the divisor removed, or halved to /9') and the fourth covers two ('either Objects.requireNonNull on the two map parameters deleted'). Four entries carry six mutants -- the same arithmetic as the round-4 'one line per mutant' with four lines for six, with 'line' changed to 'entry'. The bundling is defensible; the sentence claiming otherwise is not.
findings.failure_scenario: M0.14 lands check-mutants.sh and someone writes it to parse this file one-mutant-per-entry, on the strength of the line that says so. Two of the four entries parse as a single mutant each, so two genuine survivors -- the /9 divisor and one of the requireNonNull deletions -- count as unargued and the gate refuses a commit whose survivors are in fact all argued, or the parser is loosened and the file stops being machine-readable at all.

findings.summary: Not in this round's delta, raised because it is what the fix for the still-open finding M4.8a-tr-1 left behind and the packet asks me to verify that finding. The fixture gained two streams (RunKey(idx(3), 9) and RunKey(idx(3), 4)) and a third pod to pin the partitionId tiebreak, and three places that count it were not updated: CheckpointTest.java:33 says 'Six streams and two pods' for a fixture that builds eight streams and three pods (its own test asserts hasSize(8) at :94 and containsExactly of three podIds at :96), GoldenCheckpointTest.java:19 says 'the six streams really do carry', and ADR-0033:54 says 'measured at 148 bytes for the six-stream golden fixture'. The 148 is correct -- the golden file is exactly 148 bytes -- so only the fixture's shape is misstated, in all three places at once.
findings.failure_scenario: The golden file is re-verified by hand, which is the discipline GoldenChainEntryTest and this task's row both invoke. The verifier reads 'six streams' in the golden test's own javadoc and in the ADR, counts eight in the bytes, and concludes the golden or the fixture drifted -- the likely repair being to cut the fixture back to six, which deletes the only two streams sharing an indexId and silently unpins the partitionId leg of the comparator that finding M4.8a-tr-1 was raised to close.
